definition: Strongly bringing something to mind, or full of its scent.
example: The old railway station felt redolent of an era when travel was slow and formal.
nuance: Unlike fragrant, redolent often reaches past smell to memory, as in a town redolent of the past; it has nothing to do with indolent.
prompt: A writer describes a seaside harbor in the early morning.
options: The harbor was redolent of salt, tar, and fresh fish.
The redolent fishermen slept through the morning tide instead of hauling their nets.
The harbor was redolent of nothing, its air so clean it carried no odor at all.
The redolent sunrise glittered so brightly that the sailors had to shade their eyes.
reasons: The air is heavy with smells that call up the sea, which is just what the word conveys.
Laziness is indolence, a look-alike; redolent concerns scent and association.
Something with no scent or suggestion cannot be redolent; this reverses the meaning.
Dazzling light is resplendent; redolent is about smell or memory, not brightness.

practice.prompt: A family discovers a grandmother's handwritten recipe notebook in the attic.
options: Half the recipes were redolent, since each one had been copied out twice.
Sealed in plastic for years, the notebook was redolent of no scent or memory whatsoever.
The redolent cook hesitated for weeks before sharing her secret ingredient.
Its stained pages were redolent of cinnamon and decades of holiday baking.
reasons: Needless repetition is redundancy, a different word that only sounds similar.
Lacking any smell or association is the opposite of what the word describes.
Hesitation is reluctance; the word describes what evokes, not a person's unwillingness.
The pages carry lingering spice and call up old memories, fitting both senses.
